"family members" so that they come to tell their stories successively.
It is generally more useful to work mainly with the parent(s), i.e. the
adult alter or the host personality, in order to teach them to acquire
the necessary skills to promote communication and internal
cooperation between all the alter.
At the beginning of therapy, due to his dissociative traumatic
amnesia, the patient with an I.D.T. will first of all report a fragmented
and incoherent experience. His complete and chronological personal
history will come with time, through the gradual integration of
memories and dissociated personalities. The process of integration
can be compared to the construction of a puzzle that could not take
shape without the different pieces that make up the life experiences
that have been split by dissociation. Integration therefore consists in
assembling these puzzle pieces to recreate a coherent whole including
all the memories, whether they are valid or not. The pieces of memory
belonging to the different senses (hearing, smell, touch, sight, taste:
non-semantic memory) are managed by the hippocampus whose role
is to transfer them to thecerebral cortex so that they are processed
and integrated
consciously. Thus, they go from an unconscious mode to a conscious
mode, from a dissociated mode to an associated or re-welded mode.
They become an integrated memory which can now be verbalized
consistently[345].
The term merger is also used to describe the integration process. A
mind that has not suffered trauma and dissociation works in a unified
way. For a dissociated and fractional mind, fusion is the moment
when two (see more) alter personalities become mutually aware of
their respective existences. They then experience a kind of fusion, a
dissolution of the amnesic walls that means that they will no longer
have any separation and will therefore share the same memories. The
"final fusion" is the intended purpose of therapy. The patient passes
from a state with several identities to that of a unified subjective self,
it is unification.
It is recognized by therapists that there are three main steps in the
integration process. But above all it is absolutely necessary to
establish a feeling of physical and mental security in the patient, as
well as a stabilization and reduction of symptoms (comorbidity). This
stabilization will make it possible to work on traumatic memories,
memories that must be consciously integrated. The integration, or
fusion of alter personalities, as well as rehabilitation, are reaching the
final stage. These three steps may overlap due to an alter that might
drag out more than others, but usually the therapist treats one step
at a time.
- Phase 1: Safety, stabilization and reduction of symptoms:
First of all, it is a question of creating a kind of alliance between
the patient and the therapist to establish confidence and stability. In
this step, it is a question of minimizing behaviors that can be
dangerous for both the patient and those around him. It is also
necessary to reduce negative thoughts that can make it vulnerable to
further external attacks. The management and control of post-
traumatic stressis also a priority in Phase 1. Other behaviours that
will have to be regulated are eating disorders, risk-taking, violence,
aggression, etc. Alter personalities involved in violent behaviour and
identifying with the aggressor(s) can be particularly difficult to
manage. It is therefore a question of identifying them quickly to try to
make an agreement, a kind of contract with them to help the patient
to secure himself. These frightening, angry and violent alters often
have a protective role, despite
appearances, they are there to protect the patient.
The alter "observers" can be very useful to reconstruct
chronologically the shattered memories in order to know what
happened, the course of events (or the illusion and manipulation that
the executioners wanted to create).
Generally, alter personalities consider themselves as a truly
separated person, outside the alter group and autonomous. It is when
they become aware of the existence of other alter, that they will realize
that they are multiple and that they belong to the same physical body.
This awareness will, for example, avoid self-harm and a commitment
can be concluded with each of them to avoid self-destructive
behaviour. Many alter feel empty, depersonalized or uncertain of their
identity, it is precisely because they are only part of a whole. It is all
together that they form a complete person. It is therefore a question
of creating a form of cohesion where each alter knows the others and
finds its place in the group, or internal system.
Making alter assistants in therapy is a major asset, it is also
necessary to develop strategies to improve their understanding and
mutual communication because the patient loses a lot of energy to
have to manage internal conflicts between them. The development of
a relationship of trust and dialogue with alter personalities will be the
key to discovering trauma (phase 2) and achieving stability and
integration (phase 3).
Non-verbal and emotional communication is also an important
point. Some alter will need to be hugged, while others will take this
gesture for an attempt at sexual approach. Some alter are unable to
look straight into the eyes the person in front of them.
Some will express themselves in an extroverted way while others will
be totally terrified and will just need to listen to reassuring words.
Some can not speak, they will need to communicate through writing,
drawing or through another alter who will have a role of mediator.
The therapist should not fall into favouritism and should treat each
alter equally. Nor should he be frightened by those who seem hostile
because they use anger to protect the most vulnerable alter, who are
usually young children. During this phase, there may also be the use
of anchoring techniques in the present moment and methods of self-
hypnosis. Sometimes it will be necessary to resort to medications to
compensate for risky behaviors, but this should not be the heart of
the treatment. It is also in this first phase to develop in the patient
acceptance and empathy for each part of his split personality, each
alter must be considered for what he is and as having his role to play
in the therapy and in the life of the patient.
- Phase 2: Confrontation and integration of memories
Traumatic:
The second phase focuses on the traumatic memories of the
patient. At this level, there is still a lot of work to help him accept the
different parts of his personality and the alter must continue to get to
know each other and live together. In this stage, the work is also to
overcome the problems of blocking the patient in his past. One of the
most difficult tasks in this phase is going to be to overcome the fear
of traumatic memories in order to be able to integrate them effectively.
The patient and the therapist will have to discuss together to reach
an agreement on the memories that must be treated as a priority.
Once these traumatic memories are processed and integrated, they
must be shared with every alter personality who was not aware of
them. This pooling of traumatic experiences with all the alters of the
system is called "Synthesis". Once this Synthesis is successful, it
must continue to lead to the full awareness that the traumas have
been experienced, treated, and that they are now part of the past: it
is the "Realization". Thus the patient will be able to give a precise
place to the trauma in the chronology of his life. As a result, the pieces
of the memorial puzzle will be reconstituted little by little to form a
real chronological frieze. Synthesis is also followed by
"Personification", i.e. the awareness that these traumatic memories
belong to the patient, and to no one else. Finally, thanks to this work
on traumatic memories, the patient can transform his memories,
previously dissociated and scattered, into a coherent and
understandable narrative, it is the "Narration". It is the transition
from a non-verbal memory to a narrative and analytical memory.
During this stage, strong emotions will burst when the traumatic
content of the memories will emerge to the consciousness. The patient
may then manifest shame, horror, disgust, terror, anger,
helplessness, confusion or grief. It is then a question of giving an
adequate recovery time between each session so as not to destabilize
or retraumatize the patient. But even with careful therapeutic
planning, it may be necessary to make returns in phase 1 for a new
stabilization when the rise of a memory is particularly violent. As
traumatic experiences are integrated, alter personalities will become
less and less separate and distinct. Spontaneous fusion can also
occur but a premature global unification test can cause stress that
would be negative for the patient. As the fragmentation of the patient
subsides, he will acquire a certain inner calm with a sense of peace,
especially when the therapy is accompanied by a spiritual renewal.
Thanks to this new internal state, the patient will be better able to
understand his traumatic history and to assume the problems of
everyday life. The patient will begin to focus less on the traumas of
his past to channel his energy into the present moment, which will
help him a lot to develop new perspectives to project himself into the
future.
- Phase 3: Integration and rehabilitation:
The third phase is aimed at the integration (final unification) of the
personality. In the first two stages, the patient learned to overcome
the fear of other parts of his personality and the fear of his traumatic
memories. He also accepted and integrated the idea of having been
abused as a child. Like a painful grief, the patient will have to
abandon old beliefs to consider new perspectives. He will now have to
learn to deal with emotions that can arise such as shame, fear, terror,
anger and grief. The emotional manifestation of trauma can occur for
more than two years, as a result of which unification is considered
safe. During this period, the patient may spontaneously return to
phase 2 because new traumatic memories may still emerge. After the
final integration, the unification of all alter personalities, the patient
will usually retain the skills and attributes of the different alters that
were dissociated from his personality.
These three phases of treatment of T.D.I. are probably inspired by
the work carried out in the nineteenth century by Pierre Janet. His
psychotherapeutic method for the treatment of post-traumatic stress
included the following three steps:
1 : Stabilization of symptoms in preparation for the liquidation of
traumatic memories.
2 : The identification, exploration and modification of traumatic
memories.
3 : Relief of symptomatological residues. Reintegration and
rehabilitation of the personality. Relapse prevention.
Regarding the use of drugs, it is not a first-class treatment for
dissociative disorders, but it can have its usefulness. Indeed, some
patients require specialized treatment for substance abuse or eating
disorders. Many therapists use hypnosis, this technique is intended
to calm, soothe, contain or strengthen the "me". Hypnosis also
provides access to alter personalities that are not directly accessible
without a modified state of consciousness. Since the beginning of the
nineteenth century hypnosis has been used for the treatment of
T.D.I., it has emerged many studies demonstrating that these
patients are highly hypnotisable in comparison with other clinical
groups. The higher the hypnotistability of the individual, the more
effective it will be in therapy. Hypnosis andself-hypnosis can also be
very effective in the treatment of post-traumatic stress generally
present in patients with T.D.I..
Other specialized therapeutic methods can be useful for these
patients, such as family or expressive therapy, remodeling and
dialectical behavioral therapy (TCD), sensorimotor psychotherapy,
"primal" therapy, neuro-emotional integration by eye movements
(EMDR), etc...
EMDR (Eye Movement desensitization and reprocessing) is a
therapy of desensitization and reprocessing by the rapid movement of
the eyes, this technique first of all used to erase post-traumatic
shocks allows to treat many psychic traumas. Biofeedback or
neurofeedback devices can also be an additional aid for the patient,
as can acupuncture and even changes in food mode.
Group therapy is not recommended in the case of T.D.I., as many
of these patients find it difficult to tolerate the process that
encourages group discussions about participants' traumatic
experiences. However, from a certain stage of integration, group
energy may be an effective support for the patient. The treatment of
T.D.I. is usually done on an outpatient basis (not requiring
hospitalization), however, hospital treatment will be necessary if the
patient shows risks against himself (self-harm, suicide attempt) or
against others during the dissociative phases.
Expressive therapies will also play a positive role in the patient's
recovery. Journaling, art therapy, music therapy, horticultural and
animal therapy (especially with horses), movement therapy,
psychodrama, occupational therapy and recreational therapy offer
the patient the opportunity to apply a wide range of techniques that
can provide a means of expression and stabilization. This will
facilitate the concentration, pragmatic thinking, organization and
cooperation of the internal world (the alters). Artistic practices such
as painting, writing, collage, sculpture, etc., can serve as a visual and
palpable recording of the experience of alter personalities,
productions that can thus be examined at any time of the treatment.
To conclude this sub-chapter on therapies, here are some practical
tips and exercises[346] directly aimed at patients with dissociative
disorders:
It's about becoming aware of Tici and now." For this, it is useful to
observe and perceive oneself consciously, without making judgments.
When you notice that you are entering a dissociative state, that is,
that you are starting to leave, that you are no longer quite there, that
you perceive yourself less well, try to mark a pause. By practicing,
and perhaps even with therapeutic support, you will be able to learn
to answer the following questions:
- What situation did I find myself in when I started to dissociate
myself?
- How did I feel on the bodily and psychic levels?
- What's the last thing I remember?
- I knew I was entering a dissociative state because:
1/ I started for example to swing, to perceive myself as in a fog, to
have headaches..............................................................
2/ I stopped for example to speak, to think clearly, to be in eye
contact ...
3/ I began to tell myself that I could die, that no one could be
trusted, that I never do anything right...
- What did I try to avoid?
- What could I have done instead?
If, over time, the patient is able to answer these questions better
and better, he will be able to better control his dissociative behaviors
and will have more control over things.
What can you do when you enter a dissociative state?
- Realize that you are in a dissociative state, a state that will pass
as everything goes.
- Also be aware that this behavior occurs because it protected you
in the past. Now you don't need it anymore, you have other ways.
- Find a formula like: "Now I am an adult and in
security''. Say this sentence out loud to yourself.
- Keep your eyes open and feel the ground under your feet.
- Do you have an object that you liked (for example a plush or other
benevolent companion)? Perceive it consciously.
- Activate your senses with the help of something cold (for example,
pass ice cubes or cold water on your hands, arms, face).
- Become aware of the difference between then and now. Tell
yourself aloud the date of the day, where you are and how old you
are.
- Breathe consciously. Feel the air come in and out of your lungs.
Breathe with your eyes open, focus a little more on exhalation.
- Do something that demands your attention and activates your
senses: read or watch a picture, listen to music, touch a stone, smell
the smell of a flower or essential oil, consciously taste the aroma of a
raisin, sunflower seeds or something spicy.
- Move: walk around, shake your limbs, tap your feet, dance...
- Do something with your hands: write, paint, gardening, a puzzle,
crafts, etc.
- Take a shower and focus on water contact.
- Be understanding of yourself. You deserve to be gentle towards
yourself.
- Be sure to surround yourself with people who do you good and
with whom you do not feel threatened.
- When you are sure of this, you can say to yourself: I am now with
such and such, I know that he wants me good. If I now enter a
dissociative state, it has to do with old
memoirs. As of this moment, I am safe.
- Imagine that you put in a safe all the elements of the past that
weigh you down. Once locked up, they will no longer bother you.
5 - Development of T.D.I. in children
a/ Introduction
The T.D.I. starts in early childhood, its development will be done in
the long term and it will generally be more obvious and more
recognizable in adulthood. Dr. Greaves writes that "Personality
fractions usually manifest themselves in early childhood, as early as
2 1/2 years of age and typically around the age of 6 or 8 years[347].
In an article entitled "Incipient multiple personality in children:
Four cases", Dr. Fagan and Dr. McMahon reported the case of four
children who developed the onset of personality splitting. The
youngest was 4 years old and the oldest was 6 years old. Fagan and
McMahon state in this article that "multiplicity is around 5 years of
age until 8 years at the latest, but this will generally not be diagnosed
untiladulthood[348]."
In an article entitled "Psychotherapy with a ritually abused 3-year-
old: deceptive innocence", psychotherapist Leslie Ironside reports
that "dissociated identities were diagnosed in a child as young as
three years old, ritually abused and having endured extreme levels of
trauma[349]. ''
The existence of T.D.I. in children was established by Dr. Antoine
Despine in 1840. He reported the case of an 11-year-old Swiss girl,
Estelle, which was described earlier in this chapter. Dr. Richard Kluft
has also published several papers on children and T.D.I. including
the case of an 8-year-old child, Tom, which we will describe later.
Morris Weiss, Patricia Sutton and A.J. Utecht reported in the Journal
of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry in 1985 the case of a
10-year-old girl in an article entitled "Multiple Personality in a 10-
Year-Old Girl".
In her book "Healing The Unimaginable", Canadian therapist Alison
Miller writes: "I dealt with the case of a 10-year-old girl who had just
an alter personality in addition to her host personality, a 3-year-old
alter (...) When she was bored at school, the 10-year-old girl "went
inside her head", the 3-year-old alter then emerged and took control
of the body by behaving like a 3-year-old child, which was of course
inappropriate in a classroom. The 10-year-old girl therefore found
herself in the principal's office without having any idea what had
happened[350].
Of course, the systematic response to such behavior in a child will
be to say that it is a question of whims, a voluntary regression of the
child "who makes his baby". But dissociative disorder and dissociative
amnesia shed light on this kind of "capricious" behaviour from a
completely different point of view. Of course, children make whims
and sometimes act in a way that is not appropriate for their age, but
there are certain criteria for determining whether it is a dissociative
disorder, as in this case when the little girl does not seem to
remember her baby behavior.
Many patients reported that their alter personalities were born
during their childhood. Unfortunately in children, dissociative
disorders are usually undiagnosed for several reasons:
- Children with T.D.I. usually have secondary signs and symptoms
of the disorder. They will frequently have attention deficit,
hyperactivity, behavioural disorders, high anxiety, depression,
somatization, post-traumatic stress, dissociation and symptoms that
may appear to be psychotic in nature. Vomiting and nausea,
headache and fainting are the most common somatizations in a child.
Trance states or conversion symptoms (dissociative paralysis), which
are common in adult patients, are rarer in children. The inner voices
that the child may hear may be misdiagnosed as "schizophrenia".
- Due to the fact that dissociation and the states that may resemble
it are more common phenomena in healthy children than in healthy
adults, these dissociative symptoms can be ignored and
misinterpreted as normal child behavior.
- Intra-family abuse, a chaotic family environment and psychiatric
disorders of family members will not only complicate the diagnosis
but will also prevent proper follow-up of the child.
- But above all, the most important cause of misdiagnosis is the
insufficient training of clinicians and their lack of experience with
T.D.I.. Their disbelief about the legitimacy of this diagnosis of multiple
personality disorder will mean that they do not seek in any way to
detect its presence[351].
In children, amnesia, alternations of totally different behaviors and
hallucinations (usually auditory) are symptoms of a dissociative
disorder. Amnesia can manifest as "holes" during the day, meaning
that dissociation has occurred at some point. In adolescence, the
symptoms will begin to be more marked than in children under 11
years of age, so adolescents will be more easily diagnosed with t.d.i..
Any child with a history of physical or sexual abuse should receive an
assessment for the presence of a dissociative disorder. When the
abuse began in early childhood, was recurrent and sadistic, involved
ritual practices and the parents themselves have severe mental
disorders, then a prolonged observation of the child must be made,
as well as a history of all the encounters that the child may have had
with adults. This work must be accompanied by attentive interview
sessions to establish an accurate diagnosis. Children whose parents
themselves suffer from a dissociative disorder should be particularly
monitored on a regular basis. Several authors have reported the link
between dissociated patients and their dissociated families. The
majority of these dissociated parents themselves have a history of
physical or sexual abuse dating back to their early childhood[352]. A
vicious circle that must be understood, especially with regard to
satanic transgenerational families...
Here is a list of the child's behavioral disorders that may possibly
be related to an T.D.I.:
Intermittent depression - Trance or self-hypnotic state -
Fluctuation in intellectual abilities and moods, rapid regressions -
Amnesia - Auditory hallucinations (especially with inner voices) -
Recurrent imaginary companions - Speaking alone - Sleepwalking -
Night terrors - Sudden paralysis - Hysterical symptoms - Refers to
himself in the third person - Responds to another name, or uses
another name - Significant changes in the head onality and behaviour
- Forgetting or confusing basic and basic things - School work
fluctuating from one opposite to another - Hyper-destructive
behaviour - Self-harm - Violence against others - Suicidal words or
behaviour - Inappropriate sexual behaviour -
Social isolation, anti-social behaviour[353].
b/ The case of a three-year-old child
In September 1988, the journal "Dissociation" of the International
Society for the Trauma and Dissociation (ISSTD) published an article
describing the case of a little girl showing a dissociation of the
personality caused by repetitive traumas. The authors of this article
entitled "The development of symptoms of multiple personality
disorder in a child of three" are Dr. Richard Riley, who worked for the
U.S. Army in the Efmp (Exceptional Family Member Program) in
Belgium. , and Dr. John Mead, a private practitioner from Pasadena,
California.
The child was followed from the age of 14 months, she suffered
multiple repetitive traumas that developed in her a dissociative state.
The progression of his dissociative disorder was recorded on videotape
during a legally ordered follow-up.
Cindy (pseudonym) was first followed by Dr. Riley at the age of 14
months. It was decided that she should be examined for assessment
following a conflict between the foster family, Joan and David
(pseudonyms) and the biological mother Diane (pseudonym). Cindy
had been returned to the care of the foster family on the second day
after her birth. She had had very limited contact with her biological
mother between the ages of 3 months and 4 1/2 months, but had not
had any since.
In the first evaluation session, Cindy showed a very positive
attitude. She was curious and exploring the office, visibly cheerful
and confident. She appeared as a child receiving a lot of love and
affection, it was clear that there was a strong attachment between her
and her host family. She was also able to let the couple leave the room
without showing anxiety.
When Cindy was seen in the clinic at the age of 16 months, her
biological mother came to visit her for a few hours twice a week at the
host family's house. It was then reported that Cindy was sleeping
badly, that her appetite had deteriorated and that she was having
tantrums. Unlike the previous meeting, she was restless, she clung
to her foster mother and became very anxious when she left the room
to leave her alone with the doctor. All these findings were reported to
the judge, however custody of the child was entrusted to the biological
mother with gradual access from the foster parents so that Cindy
could adapt to the change. However, the biological mother followed
this visiting schedule very sporadically and it was learned too late
that during this period she had given birth to another baby girl, who
died of sudden infant death syndrome at the age of 3 months.
At the age of 20 months, Cindy returned to a clinical visit,
accompanied by Diane, the biological mother, and Joan, the foster
mother. Cindy had accepted everyone's company and she seemed
comfortable in this situation. At the age of 23 months, during another
visit with her foster mother, Cindy was very frightened and clinging
to her. In the months that followed, her emotional state deteriorated
completely, she insisted that she be huged and she cried if she was
not in physical contact with her foster mother. She had recurring
health problems and once arrived on a visit with a hematoma on her
earlobe. She then confessed that her biological mother had beaten
her. She also stated that she was called "Lila" by members of her
biological family. She repeatedly made it clear that her half-brother
was touching her genitals and that he was inserting objects into her
vagina. She regularly reported being physically and sexually abused.
Following these statements, a decision was made so that custody
in the biological family was only limited during the day, Cindy was
then 2 and a half years old. Her condition then improved and her
anxiety decreased, but she was still very angry and continued to cling
to her foster mother. She even wanted to sleep with her and woke up
several times a night to check that she was there. Joan reported that
the little one was talking during her sleep by repeatedly repeating "my
name is Cindy R." (the name of the host family). Cindy continued to
talk about physical and sexual abuse during day visits to her
biological family and she began to replicate these abuses on her
adopted sister, David and Joan's biological daughter...
Another medical expert was then appointed to examine the child in
the environment of his biological family. He reported that Cindy was
"cheerful and outgoing and had no abnormal or unusual behavior."
During this time, the foster mother paid an unexpected visit to Cindy
in her biological family and the little one did not seem to recognize
her or pretended that she did not know her...
The first filmed session happened when Cindy was 3 years old.
Three sessions had been scheduled to determine the state of relations
between Cindy, her biological mother and her foster family, but also
to record all the reports of abuse on videotape. She spontaneously
reiterated her testimony about the sexual abuse perpetrated by her
brothers as well as the fact that her biological family systematically
called her "Lila" instead of using her real name. At one point during a
session, she reacted when the word Lila was mentioned by saying
"What?", as if it were she who was being called. She denied her visits
to her biological family, while talking about them in a direct way. She
also reported that her biological mother called her little. When she
talked about the members of this biological family, her way of talking
about them and her behaviour became totally different. Her language
became immature, her body postures and manners were like those of
a doll. This series of video recordings was provided as evidence of ill-
treatment before the jury. As a result, the duration of childcare in the
biological family has been further reduced.
Three months later, the biological mother made a request by her
lawyer for a session with her daughter to be filmed with her: the alter
personality Lila presented herself directly during this session with the
biological mother. There were then five meetings, four of which were
recorded. During the premiere, Cindy was ready to answer any
questions about the host family without hesitation. She gave
emotional and emotional answers about the death of the foster
family's paternal grandfather, while questions about the biological
family were usually ignored or had the only answer: "I don't know."
When it was announced to her that she would return the next day for
another session, she nodded; but when it was added that she would
come with her biological mother, she first remained silent, then she
answered negatively and she ended up denying that she had just been
told that she had to do a session the next day with her biological
mother.
Following this, the child presented himself alternately with one of
the two distinct personalities, it depended on the questions that were
put to him. These personalities were those of Cindy or Lila. Lila said
she wanted to be called that, and she didn't answer questions about
the foster family or she said she didn't know. Sometimes she would
hide behind the dollhouse or chair, out of sight of her biological
mother, and Cindy could then emerge. At the end of a session, the
little one wanted to stay to put away the mess she had put in the
room, which was totally alien to Cindy's character. During the next
three sessions, Cindy and Lila appeared alternately: with the
presence of the biological mother, Lila was the active personality, but
Cindy could sometimes emerge to play aggressively while criticizing
Lilac for her behavior. Lila could answer some questions about the
foster family but she had very limited knowledge about the family.
She identified Joan R., the foster mother, as the "babysitter". In
addition to this memory gap in her personal history, Lila seemed
psychologically younger and her general knowledge was more limited
than Cindy's. When Lila made a mistake, Cindy could emerge to
correct her. Lila also had inappropriate sexual behavior in some
games. Her language was less developed than Cindy's and
phonetically more immature. An important point to point out is that
Lila didn't seem to know Cindy, while Cindy was aware of Lila, she
remembered the smallest things she had done. She didn't like him
and she didn't like anyone in her biological family. Cindy was self-
confident and dominant when she was not threatened. She also
showed guilt and remorse when her behaviour hit someone.
The video recordings of the sessions were provided as evidence but
were never used. The court explained that because not all the experts
agreed in their conclusions and recommendations, the Court did not
need these recordings. On the other hand, all the guards and the
visits with the biological mother were stopped, and a follow-up in
psychotherapy was set up for the little girl. Twelve sessions were
scheduled over a four-month period. Her foster mother was always
present and her adopted sister, Cheri, was present at three sessions.
In the first session, Cindy was showing anger against her attackers
and was encouraged to express it in her games. It was then that she
let out the fear of her biological mother. Alter Lila emerged
intermittently during this session and a few others thereafter. As the
sessions progressed, Cindy began to call her adopted sister by the
name of alter Lila. She made requests or gave him orders using the
same stern tone as her biological mother. Little by little, Cindy began
to love the alter and want Lila to live with her in the host family. She
then let the alter take part in the games more freely. The two
personalities also began to give information about the biological
family without showing anxiety. One day Cindy said that she was
older than Lila, she also strangely identified her foster mother as
"Lila's mom". During another session, Cindy responded positively to
the idea that she and Lila could get together. As a result, she seemed
to be doing much better and she started going to school. In one of the
last few sessions, she explained that she and her sister were both
Lila, but that one of them had grown faster.
The case of little Cindy therefore showed two criteria related to the
T.D.I.:
- Presence of two identities or personality states, each with its own
mode of perception, relationship with others and thought, as much
on the environment as on oneself.
- At least two of these identities or personality states take control
of the person's behavior, on a recurring basis.
Cindy and Lila are both complex personalities, each having their
own memories, their own behavior with different social relationships.
Cindy stated that she was older but also bigger than Lila. She referred
to Lila as someone separated from her and living elsewhere. Lila was

3 - The treatment of traumatic memories
a/ General
The work on traumatic (dissociative) memories is a therapeutic
process during which fragments of both psychological and physical
memories (cellular memory) are reassociated. The treatment of a
dissociative memory therefore consists in bringing together and
raising awareness of all the parts that compose it so that it is
definitively integrated, because as we have seen, the memory of a lived
experience can be broken into several pieces. Following this
integration, the emotions and physical sensations associated with
this memory will disappear to give way to a memory of what happened
similar to any other conscious memory. That is to say, the repressed
traumatic memory then becomes a chronological and
autobiographical memory no longer having any negative charge. Once
this process is complete, the different alter personalities associated
with these memories can then be merged into each other. It would
seem that in some cases, this is even done automatically as soon as
the memories are processed and made aware.
At the biological level, memories are related to different senses
(sight, hearing, smell, touch, taste but also physical pain or sexual
pleasure), they are also related to different types of emotions. These
memories are managed by the hippocampus which transmits them to
the cerebral cortex so that they are well integrated into
consciousness. This is how they pass from the unconscious level to
the conscious level. Dissociative memories remain disconnected from
consciousness, this is what is called traumatic amnesia, a "forgotten"
memory that has not been conscious. These memories can arise
abruptly and unexpectedly, usually in the form of flashbacks that are
eruptions of memories that suddenly go back to consciousness, they
can be visual, auditory, emotional and even physical. Indeed, these
rises can trigger cellular memories linked to certain areas of the body,
this can be manifested by pain, paralysis and even physical marks.
When these subconscious memories arise, they are relived as if they
were actually happening in the present moment. When a person
experiences a traumatic rise in memory resulting in a heavy
emotional state, he will absolutely need to anchor himself in the
present moment. It is then necessary that she opens her eyes (usually
closed during a flashback) and that she focuses on her direct
environment: the sounds (the voice of the therapist for example), that
she names and touches the objects around her in the room, she can
also touch her clothes by naming them one by one, etc. Anchoring
techniques are important in the work on traumatic memories, they
prevent the patient from being overwhelmed by emotion and pain.
Generally, a patient will not be ready to do this work on traumatic
memories until the system of his alter personalities is cooperative. As
we have seen before, it is necessary to establish a relationship with
the alter so that all those who have been involved in the same
experience, the same memory, can take part in the process. According
to therapist Alison Miller, a memory cannot be fully integrated (and
the programming dissolved) until all the fragments of the person
involved in the traumatic memory have aligned to share their own
piece of memory, their piece of the puzzle, in order to establish the
complete and chronological picture of the experience. In addition, if
not all fragments of the patient are cooperative, some alter can punish
those who disclose things prematurely.
Groups that practice mind control deliberately create alter
personalities who record everything and who know the entire system
with all its history. Stella Katz calls this alter the "Gatekeeper", a
guard whose function is to observe everything from the inside and
record everything without ever intervening. Once accessed, these alter
personalities can be of great help in determining both the content of

There is also the issue of traumatic memories dating back to
preverbal age, when the victim was still a baby. This type of memory
cannot be verbalized to express the experience and feelings. Between
the ages of 0 and 3 years, the declarative or explicit memory system
that requires the maturation of the hippocampus is not yet
operational. They will then be implicit memories (emotional,
behavioral, somato-sensory, perceptual, non-verbal). These implicit
memories are related to the amygdala of the right hemisphere whose
maturation
is earlier than that of the hippocampus
b/ The process of revivification
The term 'revivification' and its restoration process was described

Revivification is a tool that can be useful when it is not possible to do

When a patient has flashbacks at home, or when a memory is
"triggered" by an element of his environment, in public or in private,
he can take a notepad and write one or two words that will later be
used to refresh his memory about what triggered this dissociated
memory and the content of it. Following these few notes, he can
resume his activities without having to be constantly "harassed" by
this memory. Within 48 hours of the flashback(s), the patient is
advised to resume his notes on the trigger(s) and examine the
contents of this memory. The examination of it will be done calmly,
by a deep work of introspection, aiming to write in detail the visual
and auditory content, but also the fragrant and gustatory aspects
that are related to this traumatic memory. One criterion for
determining whether they are true dissociated memories is that they
are three-dimensional at the visual level and contain well-marked
sensory elements, such as noises and smells.
To train for this type of exercise on amnesic memories, the patient
can first practice projecting conscious and non-traumatic memories
on a "mental screen". This consists in focusing on the details of this
memory with the "eyes of the mind", that is to say closing the eyes to
imagine the scene in the most realwaypossible. In this scene, the
person can thus look, touch, feel
and taste what was present, but also listen to the sounds, words,
sentences, etc. The work can therefore begin with unsociated
memories that have not led to emotional shocks or physical pain.
Once the patient is comfortable with this "mental screen", he can
tackle memories that were previously amnesic and that are beginning
to emerge.
Here is how Brice Taylor describes the different phases of the
process:
- 1/ Take a notebook.
- 2/ The patient must have previously listed potentially triggering
elements of traumatic memory.
- 3/ The patient must be in a quiet and secure place, conducive to
treating this type of memory (preferably within 48 hours of their
emergence). He will start by referring to his list of triggers.
- 4/ It is useful for the patient to have a journal or a computer in
which he can archive the dissociated memories that have been
returned to him.
- 5/ Then the patient visualizes this memory on an imaginary
screen in his mind. He must focus on this memory thanks to his
mental eye, he will focus on the sensory system, that is to say taste,
smell, hearing, touch and sight. He must be interested in everything
that was present at the time of this traumatic experience. It must also
focus well on the words and phrases that were spoken at that time.
In people who have undergone ritual abuse and mind control, the
words spoken during dissociative states are very important because
they contain conditioning and programming. Alters who have heard
what has been said may not repeat them during such a therapy
session, they can for example tell the scene by omitting the
"soundtrack". They must then be asked to give the entire contents of
the memory, including auditory. The patient should try to see the
scene through the eyes of the alter personality(s) who experienced the
event. He does not need to relive the scene orre-experience the painful
emotions or painful sensations in the body. He just has to look at this
memory just like watching a movie on a screen, but taking great care
to recover as much information as possible. If the patient has survived
once to the traumatic event, he is now able to view it with some
hindsight for the recovery of the strict necessary: that is to say, all
the details that will help him to raise awareness of what happened
and to know which personality (s) alter (s) involved in it( s). During
this exercise, the patient does not have to judge what he sees on his
mental screen, nor should he try to modify its content. When the
patient has dissociated the emotional content of the memory, it is
then possible for him to accurately describe what he sees while the
therapist takes note of the information. He may therefore ask the
patient to slow down or repeat something without fear of traumatizing
him again. It's as if the patient has a remote control with which he
can zoom, slow down or speed up the scene, pause, rewind or stop
the story.
For this work of mental projection of a traumatic memory, the
therapist Alison Miller advises to start the story in the "normal life",
i.e. in the situation that preceded the traumatic event (for example
the trip by vehicle), and then to end it with the situation that followed
the trauma. This is intended to broaden the chronology of memory
because the alter personalities of the beginning and end of a
traumatic experience are usually not the same as those who suffered
the traumas at the heart of the story. Thus, it will help the patient to
better understand how his traumatic experiences are related to his
daily life, his autobiographical conscious memory and in what context
they took place.
- 6/ If the patient begins to experience abridgement with bodily
sensations during the visualization, he can quickly write on a piece
of paper: "My body tries to react to this memory", then thanks to the
dissociative process already very developed in him, he will deviate
from this memory which causes a physical reaction. By dissociating
himself from physical or emotional pain, he can for example
compartmentalize them in a box of his inner world. It can also replace
images that trigger abridgement with a math problem. This will allow
him to detach himself from the painful sensations because he will
then make another area of his brain work. In the event that the body
continues to react despite these measures, the patient must interrupt
his session of mental projection and anchor himself in the present
moment with the methods listed above. He can then resume the
mental projection session if he is able to maintain the dissociative
barrier between the physical and emotional bodies and traumatic
memory. The same techniques can be applied when the emotional
pain becomes too strong. During this process, the patient can also
choose to voluntarily and fully go into the emotional feeling of memory
in order to express it and make it burst as much as he can.
- 7/ If the patient feels sad, crying or angry about traumatic
memories, he can undertake another activity. A healthy young child
who falls and hurts himself will cry for a little while, but very quickly
he will fix his attention to something that will get him out of his
negative state. Children are thus able to quickly change their
emotional states. The patient can do the same by quickly choosing to
do an activity that will put him in a positive mental and emotional
state. He can do sports, garden, call a friend, walk the dog, paint,
sing, take a bath, watch a comedy, all those things that can bring him
relaxation and joy. However, this is not about repressing negative
emotions such as sadness or anger. The patient must be able to feel
and express them for as long as he needs and wishes. The patient's
healing process is largely based on the control he must have over
himself and his own experiences. This part of the revivification
process may be suitable for patients who are constantly stuck in
painful old emotions.
When survivors are able to take care of themselves and love each
other instead of self-destructing, their attackers (or controllers) have
lost. Survivors need to realize that only they can choose self-esteem
instead of scarification for example. When they stop behaving as
programming has conditionedthem, they become autonomous and
free, with only their own mind as limits: they recover their own
identity.
Brice Taylor points out that during this process it is easier to write
the traumatic memories first than to verbalize them directly. This is
also what Mark Phillips advocates, it is one of the rules he established
in Cathy O'Brien's recovery and deprogramming protocol. The act of
writing the memories causes, thanks to the coordination of the eyes
and the hand, certain neuronal connections of the brain that will give
the patient better access to his own brain abilities. In addition, writing
down the memories means that they will be much richer in detail.
Over time, the different "capsules" of traumatic memories will begin
to come together to form an overall picture highlighting what really
happened in the patient's life. This puzzle more or less well
reconstituted will explain many things that have hitherto remained
misunderstood, such as undesirable behaviors or unexplained
phobias. Brice Taylor explains that it is not necessary to dwell on
every detail of memory to know if it is valid or not, because over time
and with enough recovery of traumatic memories, the pieces of
memories will begin to validate each other by fitting together to form
the puzzle of life. It is this overview of his own life, hitherto broken
into pieces, that will help bring the patient self-compassion, self-
esteem and self-esteem so precious for his healing and his new life.
Here is an excerpt from Cathy O'Brien's book "For National
Security" which illustrates the process of recovering traumatic
memories:
"The answers only slowly come to the surface, but they bring out

Their knees? Their eyes? Simply locate the time as precisely as you

You can flip through old magazines and newspapers (...) You

Suddenly, my scribbles of memories seem to me to have an interest

Then, when I find myself in a position to concentrate properly, I let

c/ The interior theatre
In a 2006 S.M.A.R.T. lecture, survivor Lynn Schirmer described a
tool that helps focus on particular memories and can be combined
with the mental screen described earlier. It is a psychological tool that
was developed by Dr. Lowell Routley and colleagues, a model of
theater, a metaphor of consciousness and mind imagined by
neurobiologist Bernard J. Baars.
In "In the Theater of Consciousness The Workspace of the Mind",
Bernard J. Baars describes how this "theater" works that can be used
to work on memories. In a theater, there is the stage, the actors, the
projectors, the stage play, the director and the audience. When you
enter a theater before the show, you see the stage, the spectators and
a few doors on the side giving access to the boxes. As the lights begin
to go out and the audience becomes silent, a single projector pierces
in the dark to illuminate the scene. You then know that the
screenwriters, the actors, the sound and light engineers are all there,
invisible but working together in the same direction and guided by a
script that will reveal itself to the audience. While the room turns off,
only the focus of consciousness remains, i.e. the projector
illuminating the scene, everything else being in the dark. This
metaphor of the theater makes it possible to work on the memories:
the play of the actors and the sets represent the content of the
memory, traumatic or not, the projectors represent the focus of
attention on this memory, the conscious content emerges when the
spots head towards the actors on the scene of memory. These
projectors have an essential role because as soon as they direct the
light to a particular character, it emerges in consciousness. Only
these characters illuminated by the spotlight can transmit
information to the audience. In return for the audience, the audience
can applaud or whistle, ask to hear more or on the contrary evacuate
an actor from the stage by throwing tomatoes at him. The audience
of this theatre can also interact with the actors by exchanging
information with them. But there is only one way to reach the
audience as a whole, and that is through a character illuminated by
the projector on stage. The audience is the raison d'être of all this
experimental theatre.
The theater scene represents the inside of the patient, where he
experiences the different perceptions, this place is called the fusion
space. A simple exercise allows access to this place: the person must
visualize an object of his choice and try to determine where he feels
that something is happening inside him. This exercise may seem very
simple, but for MK survivors, conditioned to avoid any kind of
introspection, it may prove to be something entirely new and an
important discovery. The ability to see inside the fusion space can be
a powerful tool. With practice, it is here the person will be able to
observe the elements of the programming, in this "stage play", and
even intervene directly by himself.
The main actor of the scenario is usually the core, the real "Me",
the original personality, who can sometimes control the body. The
different actors (alter) who are not in the spotlight, who are off the
stage, represent subsets, routines, skills, memories, feelings intended
to act through particular behaviors or experiences. These different
actors can enter the stage at any time to share the star with the main
actor causing a mixing process in this fusion space. A trauma
survivor may suddenly experience severe physical pain which is
actually another part of himself stuck in a traumatic memory, with
alters being able to mix with each other. According to Lynn Schirmer,
this technique of introspection in the inner theater makes it possible
to examine this fusion space. The patient can see objects and
decorations that have been set up and used by programmers. It is a
tool for coming into contact with and interacting with the inner world.
7 - Fabian therapy
While therapies aimed at tracing dissociative memories using
hypnosis or other techniques such as EMDR (desensitization and
reprogramming by eye movement) will confront the survivor with his
traumatic past, there is a non-frontal therapeutic method that avoids
direct "contact" with painful memories. Memories that can trigger
certain implemented commands such as self-destruction and suicide
programming.
This memory processing technique was leaked by Kerth Barker, an
insider himself a survivor of satanic ritual abuse who had been
connected to the Network at some level. This therapeutic process was
transmitted to him by insiders who used their knowledge of MK
programming to develop and establish an effective and safe protocol,
aimed at discharging traumatic memories gradually, without having
to relive them directly (it would seem that in the "Family" there are
divergent opinions regarding the MK issue).
Barker named this technique : the therapy "Fabian", in reference
to the Fabian military strategy which consists in avoiding the frontal
and direct attack by setting up an indirect and progressive fight. The
purpose of this therapeutic protocol is to gradually discharge and
cancel the impact of traumatic memories, which has the consequence
of disabling the programming that relies precisely on these painful
memories repressed to a subconscious level. These dissociative
memories are toxic "capsules" that remain stuck in the subconscious,
their presence will sabotage the abilities of the individual to think
rationally and to act according to his own will. The therapeutic work
that aims to unload these unconscious toxic memories is therefore
essential to deprogram mk conditioning. This method will act on
repressed traumatic memories in an indirect way thanks to a work
carried out on conscious memories: that is to say, the sustained
stimulation of semantic and episodic memories, two distinct forms of
explicit memory.
Semantic memory is the one that contains all the information that
has been consciously memorized: telephone numbers, history
lessons, etc... This semantic memory consists of words or symbols.
Episodic memory when it consists of your life experiences. These are
the real events that you have experienced consciously, such as a walk
in the forest or a football match. This episodic memory is composed
of images, sounds, smells, tastes and emotions. Episodic memories
are therefore like films that contain sensory perceptions as well as
emotions. There is also the memory of subjective events, such as
dreams (depending on the ability of each person to remember them)
and imagination, i.e. the ability to imagine a fictitious event with the
possibility of remembering it later.
Fabian therapy is designed to avoid inappropriate triggering of
implanted programming. This type of therapy deals only with
conscious memories, i.e. episodic, semantic and subjective memories
(dreams and imagination). There will never be a direct confrontation
with dissociated and repressed traumatic memories. A sustained
work on conscious memories will be able to act indirectly on repressed
memories. Indeed, all strata of memory, down to the deepest, are
interconnected with one another in what can be called an "energy
mental field" that interacts with the brain and nervous system.
According to Fabian therapy, memories are not made up of neurons
but of a stable subatomic energy, neurons being only a physical
interface for these memory energies (all the processes that facilitate
memory operations). In this "energy field", each memory, whether
conscious or unconscious, is connected with all the others by a kind
of canvas. This means that if you work intensively on a certain area
of memory, it will automatically influence all the other areas of the
canvas: called the "memory field". By working intensively on episodic
memory, you will thus work subtly and indirectly on pain, trauma
and amnesia of other repressed memories. These dissociated
traumatic memories contain strong emotions that represent a
powerful negative emotional charge. Working on conscious memories,
in a structured and intense way, will slowly release the negative
charge of these repressed memories. When enough negative charge is
released, the implemented programs related to these memories will
cease to have power, so it will gradually release the MK slave.
The commands implemented during programming consist of words
and images, mainly words, and the words are semantic. It will
therefore be necessary to work on conscious semantic memory in
order to gradually release the negative charge of the commands
implanted in the repressed and unconscious memory. The scientists
who developed this therapy did experiments with people who had
been subjected to mind control. They were connected to a biofeedback
device measuring heart rate and breathing. The researchers then
slowly and aloud read a vocabulary list mixing neutral words and
command words typically used in MK programming. When reading,
the subject did not pay any special attention to the command words,
however whenever one of these words was spoken, the biofeedback
apparatus showed a reaction. Mk victims plugged into this device
were not aware that these words were triggers, yet they stimulate the
slave unconsciously due to the pain contained in the occulted
traumatic memory. The power of these words can be disabled by
working on vocabulary in a structured way.
Fabian therapy is divided into four areas:
- Journaling.
- The A.M.E. (Analysis of Episodic Memories), it is the systematic
analysis of certain non-traumatic conscious memories.
- The technique of extroversion.
- Vocabulary exercises to influence semantic memory, aimed at
freeing the negative charge contained in words related to implanted
commands.
a/ The newspaper
In Fabian therapy, the patient will keep three journals:
- The daily journal of episodic memory.
- The daily diary of the memory of dreams.
- The cathartic journal and the memory of the imagination.
The episodic diary: Each evening, the patient will write in this
journal his full name (the host personality), the date and an episodic
memory of the day (the meeting with an old friend, an outing to the
park ...). The memory should preferably be a striking and positive
episode, without any negative emotion. This episodic memory must
be something that has been experienced in the real world and not
something that would have been seen on television or on the Internet.
In his diary, the patient will simply describe this memory so that he
can easily remember it later. On each weekend, the patient will be
required to review all episodic memories of the week. In the same way,
at the end of the month, he will examine everything he has written in
his newspaper during these few weeks. These rereadings of episodic
memories must be done by imagining the scene as precisely as
possible in the mind, in order to record it as well as possible. This
exercise can also be done at the end of the year.
In a subtle way, this work on episodic memory participates in
discharging the negative memories weighing on the subconscious. It
is a work that requires a medium-term commitment (a few months)
or even a long-term commitment (several years) to hope for tangible
results. By detecting memory lapses on certain days, the patient will
know that a change of alter occurred that day.
The dream diary: This journal is also to be filled daily if the memory
of the dream is present. A number of people have discovered that once
they start writing their episodic journals on a daily basis, they also
start having vivid nightmares. In addition, once the patient has
undertaken an A.M.E. (Episodic Memory Analysis) on a regular basis,
this will also indirectly stimulate nightmares during sleep.
Nightmares are unpleasant, but it is rather a good sign because it is
through them that the subconscious evacuates the negative charge
contained in traumatic memories.
The patient does not have to make an analysis of his dreams in his
diary, he simply has to note its contents in the most objective way
possible, regardless of whether the dream was joyful or terrorizing.
The focus on dreams, which consists in remembering them to ask
them in writing, will also release the negative charge contained in the
memory field. It is a natural healing process of the mind.
The journal of imagination and cathartic: This journal does not
have to be kept daily but only when the patient feels the need. Its
purpose is to use imagination to release negative emotions. With this
journal, the patient will try to purge the negativity, it is not a question
of intellectualizing what is written in it because it is a purely cathartic
process. The content of the newspaper can be made up of words,
drawings, photos, etc., it is a very personal diary. The idea is to
express the bad feelings that sometimes rise for no apparent reason,
by putting them in pictures and words. It is a purely emotional and
non-intellectual process, an additional way to release the negative
emotional charge from the memory field.
b/ A.M.E. - Episodic Memory Analysis
A.M.E. is the systematic analysis of non-repressed episodic
memories. This analysis requires a therapist. These non-repressed
episodic memories are conscious memories that must not contain any
pain and negative emotion. These are the memories of ordinary and
happy experiences of everyday life. The therapist plays the role of
guide, he will ask a series of questions to help the patient to plunge
deeply into his memories. In this therapeutic process, negative
unconscious memories are indirectly influenced by this intense focus
on positive conscious memories.
The memory field is similar to a spider's web in which all memories
are connected together by wires. If you stimulate an area of the
canvas, it will stir everything else. So if you intensely stimulate an
area of the patient's conscious memory, it will more or less influence
all the other areas of memory, also dissociated memories. The
objective of this type of analysis is to ensure that the patient
consciously immerses himself in a memory to remember it as deeply
as possible in his "mental screen". The role of the therapist is to use
his intuition to guide the process by questioning the patient about
this memory in order to encourage him to dive ever deeper into it but
without ever intellectualizing anything. This protocol does not require
a hypnotic state or any altered state of consciousness, the patient just
needs to close his eyes when recalling memories. All memories worked
in A.M.E. must be of a happy nature, they must not contain any
negative emotions. In addition, it must be recent memories that have
not yet been processed, that is, raw memories that the patient has
not yet talked about. To help you understand this process, here is an
example:
- Therapist: Can you remind yourself of an appropriate memory
that we could work on today?
- Patient: I went to a football game the other day.
- T: All right. For a better memory of this memory, what was the
date and at what time did this episode begin?
- P: It happened two days ago. I think it was at 16
hours.
- T: Ok, let's start with your olfactory memory, do you remember
the smells?
- P (eyes closed): I remember the smell of popcorn in the tail where
I was waiting to buy a hot dog. There were smells of cooking, hot
dogs.... See... There was also that smell of stale beer on the floor near
the bar. When I went to the bathrooms, I remember that it smelled
very strongly of urine. In the stands, I was sitting next to a man
wearing a sickening aftershave. I also remember someone who
smoked a cigar. It was a hot day, I remember the body odors.
- T: Was it your own body odor or someone else's?
- P: There were the smells of several people. There was something
else, I'm not sure what it was.. Oh yes, my friend had put sunscreen
on his arms, he gave me a little.
- T: What was that smell like?
- P: There was a slight smell of coconut, but above all a smell of
chemicals.
- T : Well.Is there another memory of smell?
- P : Non.
- T: Okay, so now let's go over your memories regarding tastes
during this episode.
etc.
In a methodical and systematic way, each of the sensory
perceptions contained in this episodic memory, this scene of life, will
be reviewed. The therapist's questions are intended to maintain the
patient's attention and focus on the experience and his memory. A
session of this type should last from half an hour to forty-five
minutes.
The mind of a victim of MK has been altered, therefore, even the recall
of ordinary episodic memory may contain distortions. If the therapist
hears something that seems totally irrational, he does not have to
question or analyze it, he simply has to continue the process without
dwelling on it. The therapist should not make any judgments or
evaluations, he should simply help the patient maintain a focus on
the experience and his memory.
There are a number of perceptions contained in episodic memory,
Fabian therapy works with a list of eight perceptions that are as
follows:
No. 1: Olfactory (smell)
No. 2: Gustatives (taste)
N°3 : Auditory (sound)
N°4 : Tactile (touch)
N°5 : Vision (view)
N°6 : Kinetics (movements)
N°7 : Emotional (emotions)
N°8 : Linguistics (language)
The therapist will work with each of these perceptions by taking
them in the exact order of this list. These eight categories are used
sequentially, so the therapist must direct the patient to follow this
sequence in the right order. The session ends when the last category
has been reviewed. The review of the smell, taste and noises from the
beginning of the session will allow the patient to directly re-
experiment with memory without personal alteration, he will not
evaluate it but re-experiment. The review of emotions and language
will be done at the end of the session because these perceptions are
likely to be evaluated and modified by the ego. As much as possible,
the therapist should avoid mixing the different categories of memory
perceptions. For example, when analyzing category 3, which is the
memory of sounds, it would not be good to encourage the patient to
focus on the content of a conversation he has heard, because this is
what is then analyzed in category 8 (language). In category n°3, the
therapist directs the patient in the pure perception of auditory
memory. He will ask for example if the conversation was strong, sweet
with a comparison with other auditory perceptions. By focusing on
tactile perceptions (category 4) of episodic memory, the therapist can
ask these kinds of questions: "Is this hot or cold?" These perceptions
include: temperature, pressure/weight, discomfort/comfort,
moisture and dryness on the skin, satiation/hunger...

Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES)
The Scale of Dissociative Experiences
The Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) is aself-questionnaire for
adults. It was developed by Eve Bernstein Carlson and Frank W.
Putnam in 1986. The DES consists of 28 items to assess the frequency
of various dissociative symptoms in the patient's daily life. This scale
was developed to measure experiences of mental dissociation in
adults, it is the most widely used tool for the study of dissociative
disorders in psychiatry. Altered states of consciousness under the
influence of drugs or alcohol are not to be taken into account for this
test.
The final result is an average of summing the scores of the 28 items
and then dividing the number by 28. Thus we obtain a score between
0 and 100. The average DES results for the average population range
from 3.7 to 7.8. Results for psychiatric inpatients range from 14.6 to
17.0. In the Netherlands it was obtained from 71 patients suffering
from a dissociative identity disorder a score of 49.4. Patients with a
DES result of 25 or higher have a high probability of having a
dissociative disorder.
In addition to the DES, there is also the MID "Multidimensional
Inventory of Dissociation", based on the same principle but with more
than 200 items (available on the internet). The DES as well as the MID
do not allow to definitively establish a diagnosis; it is only through a
structured and thorough examination that a dissociative identity
disorder can be identified or excluded.

Introduction
What Is NLP?
Did you know that you can put a stop to your bad habits like smoking
or eating junk food through hypnosis? Think about how much this
could change your life and help you open the door to a more
prosperous life! Did you know that you can learn many new and
exciting things through NLP practices that may help you improve
yourself and your life? Although you may have been unaware, there
are many ways that you can use NLP methods to improve yourself
and your experience!
Your first question may be, “What exactly is NLP or Neuro-Linguistic
Programming?” You may have never even heard this term before, let
alone know what it means and what it’s all about! This is a fair and
essential question! When learning about any new topic, it’s vital to
understand the foundations of it. This could not be truer for the issue
of NLP as well!
Neuro-Linguistic Programming was created in the 1970s by a pair of
self-help trainers in California. It is an approach that attempts to aid
communication skills, psychotherapy, and personal development.
Based on the idea of this therapy, there is a connection between our
brains (neuro), language (linguistic), and learned behavioral patterns
(programming). It is believed these three things can be changed to
alter and, hopefully, improve one’s behavior or accomplish specific
goals. The creators of this approach, as well as many others who
practice or use it, claim that an entire slew of issues, problems, and
obstacles in life can be solved through this self-help therapy.
Depression, addictions, phobias, allergies, the common cold, or
learning disorders are just a few that are believed to be treatable
through this therapy. There have even been claims that some have
been treated in as short as a single session!
There are also many different strategies and types of Neuro-
Linguistic Programming, and in the coming chapters, we will explore
how you can implement them into your life to make positive changes
that will, hopefully, lead to outstanding personal success! A few of
these strategies are hypnosis, memory alterations, and reframing.
Although these may seem like very foreign and even strange
concepts to you now, don’t worry! This book will help you to explore
many of the different NLP topics and help you to understand just
what they are! Let’s begin!
In this section, we are going to take some time to shift our focus and
spend a bit of time looking at NLP. The idea of NLP, known as neuro-
linguistic programming, was first developed by Richard Bandler and
John Grinder in 1976. This is going to be comprised of three parts
including the neuro that is going to focus on the neurology, the
linguistics that will reference back to language, and then
programming that will refer to the function of that neural language.
These men spent some of their time studying three individuals and
their ability to change up the feelings and thoughts that they had.
Over the years, many have adopted these ideas, although there is
some criticism out there that looks at the legitimacy of the results of
the study.
NLP is more of a thought, rather than a process, that can be used on
other people. It is more of something that you should concentrate on
yourself. The basic ideas that come with NLP are that you want to
change the thoughts and the feelings that are inside yourself. Doing
this is excellent for those who would like some relief from things like
depression, anxiety, and some of the other mental illnesses that are
out there. These individuals may feel that there is a specific thought
or another belief that is holding them back, and when they can make
changes to these things, the individual can change their life.
An excellent example of this would be when someone decides to
make themselves believe that they like exercising, even if they
disliked it ahead of time. Some people have found that using the
tactics that come with NLP can bring them some success. But some
have criticized the capabilities of this process and how well it can
work for those who choose to use it .
There are going to be some benefits that come with neurolinguistics
programming, no matter what side of the debate you are on, but
there are some issues because it can be used as a tactic for
manipulation. NLP intends to be able to look inward to figure out
what makes the person unique and their person. The things that
form the beliefs of that person are also going to indicate the quality
of life they are going to have. The idea here is that by changing up
these beliefs, it is easier for that person to change or improve
different parts of their life.
Some manipulators will learn about the NLP ideas and then will use
these in more dangerous manners. These manipulators are going to
use some of the tactics that come with NLP to try and convince their
victims to do things that may harm the victim, but which are going to
benefit the manipulator in one way or another.

going to work on their body language to get the message across a

such as standing tall or using a lot of gestures that show anger,
excitement, and more to increase the impact of what they are saying.
Surprises That Are Done in a Negative Manner
Some manipulators like to work with surprises that are considered
harmful to put their victims off balance, and because it allows them
to gain the psychological advantage. There are several ways that the
manipulator can do this. They could low ball during a situation of
negotiations, or the manipulator could have a sudden profession that
they won’t be able to come through and do the thing that they had
promised before.
In most cases, the unexpected negative information is going to come
to the victim without any warning. This makes it hard for the victim to
prepare and try to counter the move in the way that they would like.
In the end, the manipulator could ask for some additional
concessions from their victim to continue working together.
Limiting the Amount of Time to Decide
One technique that can be useful for a manipulator is to limit the
amount of time that the other person gets to make a decision. When
the victim feels like they are limited to time, they are more likely to go
along with what the manipulator wants, even though not sure about
the decision and they were not provided enough time to think it all
through, and this is what the manipulator wants to see happening.
The idea of giving the victim little time to decide on things is a
collective negotiation and sales tactic. This is where the manipulator
is going to put some pressure on the other person to make up their
decision, often before the victim is ready to make that decision.
When you apply the tension and the control over the other person,
the hope is that they are going to crack and then they will give in to
the demands of the aggressor.
Poking at Your Weaknesses
Some manipulators are fond of making critical remarks, but then will
disguise these remarks as sarcasm and humor. They can do this to
make their victim feel inferior and less secure, but the fun helps the
manipulator to save face and look better when the victim starts to get
offended. In the process, they can make the victim seem less secure
and inferior.
There are a lot of examples that come to mind with this one. The
manipulator can have comments that will range from your personal
belongings, your credentials and background, your appearance, and
the fact that you came into the office just a few minutes late and
seemed to be out of breath. The manipulator likes to point out the

superiority over the victim .
Criticism and Judgment Against You
This behavior is going to be distinct from some of the other practices
that we have discussed. In those, humor was a kind of cover that the
manipulator could use to say what they want, and then turn it back
against the victim. However, with this one, the manipulator is doing
away with the joking and is outright just picking on their victim.
By continually marginalizing, ridiculing, and dismissing their victim,
the manipulator can keep their victim off-balance, while also making
sure that they, the manipulator, can maintain their superiority. The
aggressor would use this tactic to deliberately foster the impression
that there is something always wrong with their victim, and that no
matter how hard the victim tries, they are going to be inadequate and
never good enough to meet the standards of the manipulator.
The thing here is that the manipulator only wants to focus on the
negative and the bad things that go on. With regular criticism, there

that the victim can work on. With manipulation, the manipulator is
just going to focus on the negative without giving any constructive or
genuine solutions, and they never offer any meaningful ways to help
the other person. They like to say and do things that will make the

Using the Silent Treatment
We are all guilty of using this one at some point. We will get mad at

Many manipulators are going to use this tactic as well. By
